[notes-n1] Notes 1. Foundations: types and requirements
A foundation carries the loads of the building into the ground. Every soil compresses under load, so every building settles. The design keeps the total settlement small, and the difference between neighbouring columns smaller still, by bearing on a stratum that is strong enough and by spreading the load over a large enough area (course notes).
Two checks at two load levels The soil. Under the service loads, G_k + Q_k, the bearing pressure must not exceed the allowable bearing pressure q_{all}. The geotechnical engineer sets q_{all} with a factor of safety against bearing failure already inside it (typically 2.5 to 3) and low enough to keep the settlement acceptable, so the loads are not factored again. The concrete. The base is designed at the ultimate limit state, 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k, for bending, shear and punching, like any other member (EC2).
[Figure: The six types of foundation of the course notes. Units 10 to 12 design all of them except the raft.]
Type Use it when Unit
Pad footing One column on ground strong enough near the surface. The simplest and cheapest base: square or rectangular in plan, one thickness. 10
Strip footing A load-bearing wall; a row of columns too close for separate pads; or weak ground that needs more bearing area. 10
Combined footing Two columns so close that their pads would overlap, or a column at the site boundary. The base is placed so that its centroid lies under the resultant of the loads. 10
Strap footing A boundary column whose pad cannot project past the boundary: a strap beam ties it to an inner footing to resist the overturning. 11
Raft Heavy loads or low bearing pressure, or variable ground with compressible layers: one slab under the whole building limits the differential settlement. not in this course
Piles and pile cap Firm ground deeper than about 3 m: piles carry the load down by end bearing, by friction, or both. 11–12
The course takes the pressure under a rigid base as linear: uniform under a central load, sloping when there is a moment. Real pressure is higher at the edges on clay and higher at the centre on sand (course notes); the straight line is the design convention, and it is what EC2 designers and the RC Design app use.
Cover on the casting face (EC2 4.4.1.3(4)) c_{nom} = c_{min} + Δc_{dev} as in RCD I, and not less than 40 mm when the base is cast on prepared ground or blinding, or 75 mm when it is cast directly against the soil. The course notes’ Example 1 stops at 35 mm; on blinding, 40 mm governs (Worked Example 10.1).
For your project the 2024/25 brief gives 2 m of made ground over mudstone with an allowable bearing pressure of 600 kN/m². Made ground is fill: variable and compressible, so no footing should bear on it. Two answers are open: pads taken down through the fill to the mudstone, or piles. The studio asks you to choose with numbers.
Quick check (not graded): A pad footing is cast on a 50 mm layer of blinding. c_{min} = 25 mm and Δc_{dev} = 10 mm. The nominal cover is
Options: 35 mm | 40 mm | 50 mm | 75 mm
Explanation shown after answering: c_{min} + Δc_{dev} = 35 mm, but EC2 4.4.1.3(4) asks for at least 40 mm on blinding. 75 mm applies when the concrete is cast directly against the soil; the blinding thickness does not enter.
Key points:
- Pad for one column, strip for a wall, combined for two close columns; strap, raft and piles when these do not fit.
- Soil: service loads against q_{all}. Concrete: ultimate loads, EC2.
- c_{nom} ≥ 40 mm on blinding, ≥ 75 mm against the soil.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. Sizing the base
Sizing comes first and uses the service loads; the depth and the bars come next and use the ultimate loads. Keep the two apart and most footing slips disappear.
EQUATION (10.1): A_{req} = \frac{G_k + Q_k + W}{q_{all}},\qquad W \approx 0.1\,(G_k + Q_k)\ \text{at first, then } W = 25\,A\,h
Choose the plan to the nearest 0.1 m above A_{req}, then recompute W with the chosen size and check p = (G_k + Q_k + W)/A ≤ q_{all}. If only design loads are given, the course divides them by γ_F ≈ 1.4 to get service loads (course notes, Examples 2 and 3). Mosley does the same sum the other way round: the net allowable pressure q_{all} − 25h carries G_k + Q_k alone.
EQUATION (10.2): p_{Ed} = \frac{N_{Ed}}{A},\qquad N_{Ed} = 1.35\,G_k + 1.5\,Q_k
The ultimate pressure leaves the self-weight out. The weight of the base rests on the soil directly below it, so it bends nothing and shears nothing; only the column load, spread by the base, does (Mosley §10.1). Adding 1.35W to N_{Ed} overstates every moment and shear in the base.
The depth Bending rarely decides the depth of a footing; shear does, by punching or by vertical shear at d. Choose a trial h, design, and deepen the base if a shear check fails. The column face sets a floor, d ≥ N_{Ed}/(v_{Rd,max}u_0) (course notes), and the starter bars need their compression anchorage within h (Mosley §10.1). For Worked Example 10.1 the floor is 1410 × 10³/(3.60 × 1200) = 326 mm; the punching check needs more.
Worked Example 10.1 Output
Service load G_k + Q_k = 600 + 400 1000 kN
Area required (1000 + 100)/150 7.33 m²
Plan chosen 3.0 × 3.0 m, h = 500 mm A = 9.0 m²
Self-weight 25 × 9.0 × 0.50 112.5 kN
Service pressure (1000 + 112.5)/9.0 123.6 ≤ 150 kN/m² ✓
Ultimate pressure (1.35 × 600 + 1.5 × 400)/9.0 = 1410/9.0 156.7 kN/m²
Quick check (not graded): A column brings G_k + Q_k = 1000 kN onto soil with q_{all} = 150 kN/m². Taking the self-weight as 10% at first, the area required is
Options: 6.67 m² | 7.33 m² | 10.3 m² | 9.00 m²
Explanation shown after answering: (1000 + 100)/150 = 7.33 m². 6.67 forgets the self-weight; 10.3 sizes the base with the ultimate load 1410 kN, which double-counts the factor of safety; 9.00 m² is the 3.0 × 3.0 m plan that is then chosen.
Key points:
- Plan area from the service loads and q_{all}, with the self-weight; check the pressure with the real self-weight.
- Ultimate pressure p_{Ed} = N_{Ed}/A, without the self-weight.
- Shear, not bending, usually sets the depth.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. The pressure when the load is off-centre
Today’s big question. Press a foam block through a stiff plate: at the centre it sinks evenly; move your finger off-centre and one edge sinks more; move it far enough and the far edge of the plate lifts off the foam. The soil under a footing does the same, and the numbers follow from equilibrium alone.
[Figure: The hook: the further the load moves off-centre, the more the pressure tilts, until part of the base lifts off.]
EQUATION (10.3): e = \frac{M}{N}\qquad \left(N = G_k + Q_k + W \text{ for the soil check};\ N = N_{Ed} \text{ at the ultimate limit state}\right)
A moment on the base moves the resultant of the load off the centre by e. As long as the whole base stays in contact, the pressure is that of a short column, axial load plus bending, with the plan of the base as the section (Mosley Eq. 10.2 and 10.3):
EQUATION (10.4): p_{max,\,min} = \frac{N}{A} \pm \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{N}{A}\left(1 \pm \frac{6e}{L}\right),\qquad Z = \frac{B L^2}{6} \qquad (e \le L/6)
At e = L/6 the minimum pressure reaches zero and the diagram is a triangle with p_{max} = 2N/A: the resultant sits on the edge of the middle third, the kern. Beyond L/6 the formula would give a tension under the low edge, which soil cannot give. That part of the base lifts off, and the pressure becomes a triangle over a contact length L_c whose centroid lies under the load: L_c/3 = L/2 − e.
EQUATION (10.5): L_c = 3\left(\frac{L}{2} - e\right),\qquad p_{max} = \frac{2N}{B\,L_c} \qquad (e > L/6)
[Figure: The three cases, and the kern: a resultant inside the rhombus keeps every part of the base in contact.]
Worked numbers: a base that lifts off (app case F3) A 2.4 × 2.0 m base carries N_{Ed} = 600 kN and M_{Ed} = 300 kN m along its length: e = 300/600 = 0.50 m > L/6 = 0.40 m. Eq. (10.4) would give 125 ± 156 = 281 and −31 kN/m², a pull the soil cannot give. Instead L_c = 3(1.20 − 0.50) = 2.10 m and p_{max} = 2 × 600/(2.0 × 2.10) = 286 kN/m²; the last 0.30 m lifts off. Under service loads with the self-weight, e = 214.3/500.6 = 0.43 m, still past L/6: L_c = 2.32 m and p_{max} = 216 ≤ 250 kN/m² ✓. EC7 6.5.4 asks for special precautions once e exceeds L/3, when less than half the base is in contact.
With moments about both axes the pressure is largest at one corner, and every corner stays in contact while the resultant lies inside the kern, a rhombus with its corners at L/6 on each axis:
EQUATION (10.6): p = \frac{N}{A} \pm \frac{M_x}{Z_x} \pm \frac{M_y}{Z_y},\qquad \text{all corners in contact if } \frac{6e_x}{L_x} + \frac{6e_y}{L_y} \le 1
Checking e_x ≤ L_x/6 and e_y ≤ L_y/6 separately is not enough: with e_x/L_x = e_y/L_y = 1/8 each passes, yet 6/8 + 6/8 = 1.5 and a corner lifts off. App case F4, a 2.5 m square pad under N_{Ed} = 900 kN with 120 and 80 kN m, gives 220.8 and 67.2 kN/m² at the opposite corners, with 6e_x/L_x + 6e_y/L_y = 0.47. Where one moment dominates, a rectangular base long in that direction is the economical shape (Mosley §10.1).
Quick check (not graded): A base 2.4 m long carries N = 600 kN at e = 0.5 m from its centre. The length of the base in contact with the soil is
Options: 2.40 m | 2.10 m | 1.40 m | 0.70 m
Explanation shown after answering: e = 0.5 m > L/6 = 0.4 m, so part of the base lifts off: L_c = 3(1.2 − 0.5) = 2.10 m. 2.40 m would need e ≤ L/6; 1.40 m is L − 2e, the effective width of a bearing-capacity calculation, not the contact length; 0.70 m is L/2 − e alone.
Key points:
- e ≤ L/6: p = (N/A)(1 ± 6e/L), a trapezoid. e = L/6: a triangle, 2N/A to zero.
- e > L/6: part of the base lifts off; L_c = 3(L/2 − e), p_{max} = 2N/(BL_c). Beyond L/3, special precautions (EC7 6.5.4).
- Two moments: corner pressure N/A ± M_x/Z_x ± M_y/Z_y; kern 6e_x/L_x + 6e_y/L_y ≤ 1.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. Critical sections: bending, shear, punching
A pad footing is a short, thick cantilever slab turned upside down: the soil pushes up, the column holds it down. It is checked where it bends most, where it shears as a beam, and where the column tries to punch through it.
[Figure: The critical sections of a pad footing. Under a column base EC2 6.4.4(2) adds every perimeter closer than 2d.]
Bending at the column face. The moment is taken on a section right across the base, from the pressure on one side of it. With l = (L − c)/2, the cantilever from the face:
EQUATION (10.7): M_{Ed} = p_{Ed}\,B\,\frac{l^2}{2}\quad\text{(uniform)};\qquad M_{Ed} = B\left[p_f\,\frac{l^2}{2} + \left(p_{max} - p_f\right)\frac{l^2}{3}\right]\quad\text{(linear, } p_f \text{ at the face)}
Two layers of bars cross. In a square pad the course takes the inner layer’s d = h − c − 1.5φ for both directions, which is safe; in a rectangular pad the bars for the larger moment go in the outer layer, d_x = h − c − 0.5φ, and the others above them, d_y = h − c − 1.5φ. Then RCD I: K = M/(f_{ck}bd²), z ≤ 0.95d, A_s = M/(0.87f_{yk}z), and A_{s,min} = 0.26(f_{ctm}/f_{yk})bd ≥ 0.0013bd (EC2 9.2.1.1). Footings are lightly stressed, so the minimum often governs: in Faded Example 10.2 it governs both ways.
Vertical shear at d from the face (EC2 6.2.1(8)). The shear is the pressure beyond the section, resisted by the concrete alone:
EQUATION (10.8): V_{Ed} = p_{Ed}\,B\,(l - d);\qquad V_{Rd,c} = \left[0.12\,k\,(100\rho_l f_{ck})^{1/3}\right] b\,d \ \ge\ v_{min}\,b\,d,\quad v_{min} = 0.035\,k^{3/2} f_{ck}^{1/2}
The bars count in ρ_l only if they run at least l_{bd} + d beyond the section (EC2 Figure 6.3). The section at d is often closer than that to the edge of a footing, so ρ_l = 0 and v_{min} is the whole resistance: in Worked Example 10.1 the bars have 868 mm beyond the section and need 485 + 442 = 927 mm.
Punching. The basic control perimeter lies at 2d from the column, with rounded corners. The soil pressure inside it pushes straight back on the column, so it does not punch; only the rest does (EC2 Eq. 6.48). d is the mean of the two layers.
EQUATION (10.9): u(a) = 2(c_1 + c_2) + 2\pi a,\quad A(a) = c_1 c_2 + 2a(c_1 + c_2) + \pi a^2;\qquad V_{Ed,red} = N_{Ed} - p_{Ed}\,A(a),\quad v_{Ed} = \frac{\beta\,V_{Ed,red}}{u\,d}
Column bases: every perimeter inside 2d (EC2 6.4.4(2)) For a column base the check is made at every a ≤ 2d, with the resistance raised as the perimeter closes in, v_{Rd} = v_{Rd,c} · 2d/a (Eq. 6.50). A closer perimeter is shorter and keeps more of the load, but its resistance rises faster, so the worst lies in between, usually near a = d (between about 0.75d and 1.25d in this Unit’s examples). By hand, check a = d as well as 2d; the Foundation Lab and the app scan 400 perimeters.
EQUATION (10.10): v_{Rd}(a) = v_{Rd,c}\,\frac{2d}{a}\qquad (a \le 2d)
[Figure: The punching scan of Worked Example 10.1. With the course notes’ h = 450 mm the check at 2d passes, yet the base fails at a ≈ 1.2d; h = 500 mm passes everywhere.]
With a moment the shear round the perimeter is uneven, and β raises the peak: β = 1 + k(M_{Ed}/V_{Ed})(u_1/W_1) (EC2 Eq. 6.39), with k from Table 6.1 (c_1/c_2 = 0.5, 1, 2, 3 gives 0.45, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80; interpolate) and W_1 = c_1²/2 + c_1c_2 + 4c_2d + 16d² + 2πdc_1 (Eq. 6.41). For a perimeter at a, 2d becomes a: W = c_1²/2 + c_1c_2 + 2c_2a + 4a² + πac_1.
EQUATION (10.11): v_{Ed,0} = \frac{\beta\,N_{Ed}}{u_0\,d} \le v_{Rd,max} = 0.4\,\nu\,\frac{f_{ck}}{1.5},\qquad \nu = 0.6\left(1 - \frac{f_{ck}}{250}\right)
At the column face the strut capacity limits the stress (EC2 6.4.5(3)). The course uses 0.4νf_{cd}, the value of the 2014 amendment of EC2; the course notes keep 0.5νf_{cd} from the 2004 text.
Quick check (not graded): Under a column base, v_{Rd,c} = 0.38 N/mm². On the perimeter at a = d the design resistance is
Options: 0.19 N/mm² | 0.38 N/mm² | 0.76 N/mm² | 3.60 N/mm²
Explanation shown after answering: v_{Rd} = v_{Rd,c} · 2d/a = 0.38 × 2 = 0.76 N/mm² (EC2 Eq. 6.50). 0.38 is the resistance at 2d; forgetting 2d/a makes a sound base look as if it fails (Exercise C2). 3.60 N/mm² is v_{Rd,max} at the column face for C25/30.
Key points:
- Bending at the column face over the whole width; shear at d; punching at 2d with V_{Ed,red} = N_{Ed} − p_{Ed}A.
- Column bases: every a ≤ 2d, v_{Rd} = v_{Rd,c}·2d/a; the worst is usually near a = d.
- ρ_l counts only bars anchored l_{bd} + d beyond the section; often v_{min} governs.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. Combined footings
When two columns stand close together, or one stands on the site boundary, one base carries both. Place it right and the pressure under it is uniform; design it as a beam turned upside down.
EQUATION (10.12): \bar{x} = \frac{N_B\,s}{N_A + N_B}\ \ \text{(service loads, from column A)};\qquad \text{centroid of the base at } \bar{x} \ \Rightarrow\ p \text{ uniform}
Choose the area from Eq. (10.1) with both loads, then the length L so that the centre of the rectangle sits under the resultant; the width B follows. If the boundary stops the base short of that, the base becomes a trapezoid (Unit 11).
Along the length the base is a beam loaded upward by w = p_{Ed}B (kN/m) and held down by the two columns. With x from the left end and the column loads at x_A and x_B:
EQUATION (10.13): V(x) = w\,x - \sum N_i,\qquad M(x) = \frac{w\,x^2}{2} - \sum N_i\,(x - x_i);\qquad V = 0 \text{ between the columns at } x_0 = \frac{N_A}{w}
Positive M puts the bottom in tension: under the columns and in the two cantilevers. Between the columns the base hogs, the top is in tension, and the largest hogging moment is at x_0. So a combined footing needs bars in both faces along its length.
[Figure: App case F6 (course notes Example 3): the shear force and bending moment along the base, by Eq. (10.13).]
Case F6 Output
Resultant (service) x̄ = 1392.9 × 3.4/2542.9 1.86 m from A
Base L = 6.0 m centred on x̄; B = 2.7 m left end 1.14 m from A
Upward load w = (1610 + 1950)/6.0 593.3 kN/m
Zero shear x_0 = 1610/593.3 2.71 m
Hogging, top bars 593.3 × 2.71²/2 − 1610 × (2.71 − 1.14) −352.8 kN m
Sagging at the faces of B from Eq. (10.13) 430 · 473 kN m
Bars A_{s,min} = 2722 mm² governs top and bottom 25H12 · 25H12
Across the width , under each column, the base cantilevers (B − c)/2 each side and is designed per metre, M = p_{Ed}l²/2: under column A of F6, 219.8 × 1.2²/2 = 158 kN m/m, and A_{s,min} gives H12-100. The shear is checked at d from each column face across the full width, from the diagram; the punching perimeter of each column stops at a free edge and runs straight to it (EC2 6.4.2(4), Figure 6.15). Under column B of F6, 2d = 1196 mm reaches past both long edges, 1150 mm away, so the perimeter becomes two lines across the base, u = 2 × 2700 = 5400 mm.
Quick check (not graded): A rectangular combined footing carries two columns, with uniform pressure under it. Where must its top face be reinforced for tension?
Options: under each column | between the columns | in the two cantilever ends | nowhere: the whole base is in compression
Explanation shown after answering: Between the columns the upward pressure bends the base like a beam spanning from column to column, so it hogs and the top is in tension (−352.8 kN m in F6). Under the columns and in the cantilevers the bottom is in tension.
Key points:
- Centroid of the base under the resultant of the service loads: uniform pressure.
- Lengthwise an upside-down beam: top bars between the columns (hogging at V = 0), bottom bars under them.
- Crosswise cantilevers under each column; punching perimeters stop at the free edges.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. Strip footings and detailing
A wall needs a strip footing, designed one metre at a time; and every footing needs its bars anchored, spaced and covered so that the design actually works on site.
Strip footing under a wall. Per metre run, the base is a cantilever on each side of the wall. For a concrete wall the bending section is at the wall face; for a masonry wall the RC Design app takes it halfway between the face and the centre line, the conservative practice of ACI 318, because a masonry wall is less rigid than the footing. App case F5:
Case F5: 230 mm brick wall, G_k 120 + Q_k 60 kN/m Output
Width (180 + 18)/150 = 1.32 m → B = 1.4 m; p = (180 + 12.3)/1.4 137 ≤ 150 kN/m² ✓
Ultimate pressure (1.35 × 120 + 1.5 × 60)/1.4 = 252/1.4 180 kN/m²
Bending section l = (1.4 − 0.23)/2 + 0.23/4 0.643 m
Moment 180 × 0.643²/2 37.2 kN m/m
Bars A_s = 306, A_{s,min} = 392 mm²/m governs; spacing ≤ 2h and ≤ 250 mm H12-250 across, H10-300 along
Shear at d from the same section: 180 × 0.349 63 ≤ 127 kN/m ✓
A line load has no punching perimeter: the vertical shear is the shear check (Mosley §10.4).
[Figure: Detailing a pad (left) and a strip footing whose bars cannot anchor straight near the edge (right).]
Detailing checklist (EC2 9.8.2, Mosley §10.1, course notes) Anchorage. Bars run the full length and width and are anchored beyond every critical section. Near the edge, EC2 9.8.2.2 asks that the bar force at x from the edge, F_s = Rz_e/z_i, anchor within x; straight bars usually pass in a pad (in Worked Example 10.1 they need 0.73 of the length available), but the strip of F5 needs its bars bent up. Spacing. Spread the bars evenly across a square base. In a rectangular base Mosley and the course notes put at least two-thirds of the short-direction bars in a band c + 3d centred on the column; EC2 itself sets no band. Cracks. σ_s under the quasi-permanent load, (G_k + 0.3Q_k)/N_{Ed} × (f_{yk}/1.15) × A_{s,req}/A_{s,prov}, gives the largest spacing from Table 7.3N (w_k = 0.3 mm), interpolated; the spacing provided is (b − 2c − φ)/(n − 1). Faces and starters. No bars in the top or side faces unless part of the base lifts off or is lifted; cover 40 mm on blinding, 75 mm on soil; starter bars bent 90° and tied to the bottom mat, with a kicker and the lap measured from its top.
Quick check (not graded): Under the quasi-permanent load the bars of a pad work at σ_s = 213 N/mm². Table 7.3N (w_k = 0.3 mm) gives 250 mm at 200 N/mm² and 200 mm at 240 N/mm². The largest bar spacing is about
Options: 250 mm | 233 mm | 200 mm | 300 mm
Explanation shown after answering: 250 − (213 − 200)/40 × 50 = 233 mm. Reading the next row down, 200 mm, is safe but wasteful; 250 mm is on the unsafe side. The 24H12 of the course notes’ Example 1 are 127 mm apart.
Key points:
- Strip footing: per metre; bending at the wall face, or halfway to the centre line for masonry; no punching.
- Anchor the bars beyond each critical section and near the edge (EC2 9.8.2.2); bend them up when straight bars cannot.
- Spacing from Table 7.3N at σ_s under the quasi-permanent load; cover 40/75 mm; starter bars with a kicker.

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions
Exam type short written answers Time ≈ 3 min each
Questions
- Why is the self-weight of the base left out of the pressure used for bending and shear, but kept in the bearing-pressure check?
- When e > L/6, why is N/A ± M/Z wrong, and what happens to the pressure instead?
- Why does EC2 ask a column base to be checked for punching at perimeters inside 2d, when a slab is usually checked at 2d?
- Why is a combined footing placed with its centroid under the resultant of the loads, and where does it need top bars?
Write your four answers first, then open the model answers one by one.
## Answer 1 Who carries the weight
The base presses on the soil with its own weight, so the bearing check must include it: the soil feels the column load plus the base. But each part of the base rests on the soil directly below it; its weight is balanced on the spot and bends nothing. The moments and shears in the base come only from the column load being spread outwards, so p_{Ed} = N_{Ed}/A (Mosley §10.1). Adding 1.35W overstates every moment and shear.
## Answer 2 Soil cannot pull
Beyond L/6 the formula gives a negative pressure under the low edge: a tension the soil cannot give. That edge lifts off instead. The pressure becomes a triangle over a contact length L_c, and equilibrium sets it: the triangle must carry N, and its centroid, L_c/3 from the high edge, must sit under the load, so L_c = 3(L/2 − e) and p_{max} = 2N/(BL_c). In case F3, 286 kN/m² instead of 281, with the last 0.30 m off the ground. Beyond L/3 EC7 asks for special precautions.
## Answer 3 The relief from the soil
Under a column base the soil pushes up inside the perimeter, and that part of the load never crosses it: V_{Ed,red} = N_{Ed} − p_{Ed}A(a). At 2d the area is large and the relief is large, so a base can pass at 2d and still fail closer in, where the perimeter is short and nearly the whole column load crosses it. EC2 6.4.4(2) therefore checks every a ≤ 2d, with the resistance raised by 2d/a for the steeper failure surface. In a slab the load inside 2d is small, so the basic perimeter usually governs. Worked Example 10.1 with h = 450 mm passes at 2d and fails at 1.2d.
## Answer 4 Uniform pressure, then a beam upside down
With the centroid under the resultant, the load has no eccentricity on the base, so the pressure is uniform: no edge is overloaded and the base settles evenly. Lengthwise the base is then a beam with a uniform upward load, held down at the two columns. Between the columns it hogs, so the top is in tension there, with the largest moment where the shear is zero (x_0 = N_A/w; −352.8 kN m in F6). Under the columns and in the cantilevers the bottom is in tension.

[glossary-allowable-bearing-pressure-q-all] Glossary: allowable bearing pressure q_{all}
allowable bearing pressure q_{all}: The pressure the soil may carry under service loads, set by the geotechnical engineer with a factor of safety against bearing failure (typically 2.5 to 3) and a limit on settlement.

[glossary-basic-control-perimeter-u-1] Glossary: basic control perimeter u_1
basic control perimeter u_1: The punching perimeter at 2d from the column face, with rounded corners: 2(c_1 + c_2 ) + 4πd (EC2 6.4.2).

[glossary-bearing-pressure] Glossary: bearing pressure
bearing pressure: The pressure between the base and the soil; taken as linear under a rigid base.

[glossary-blinding] Glossary: blinding
blinding: A thin layer of lean concrete laid on the excavated ground so that the base can be cast clean and level; on blinding c_{nom} ≥ 40 mm (EC2 4.4.1.3(4)).

[glossary-column-base-punching] Glossary: column base (punching)
column base (punching): A footing or pile cap under a column; EC2 6.4.4(2) checks it at every perimeter a ≤ 2d with v_{Rd} = v_{Rd,c} ·2d/a.

[glossary-combined-footing] Glossary: combined footing
combined footing: One base under two columns, placed so that its centroid lies under the resultant of their loads.

[glossary-contact-length-l-c] Glossary: contact length L_c
contact length L_c: The length of base still pressing on the soil when e > L/6: 3(L/2 − e).

[glossary-critical-section] Glossary: critical section
critical section: A section where a base is checked: the column face (bending), d from the face (shear), the perimeters up to 2d (punching).

[glossary-differential-settlement] Glossary: differential settlement
differential settlement: The difference in settlement between parts of a building, which cracks it; limited by sound bearing and by tying the base together.

[glossary-eccentricity-e] Glossary: eccentricity e
eccentricity e: M/N: how far the resultant of the load lies from the centroid of the base.

[glossary-kern-middle-third] Glossary: kern (middle third)
kern (middle third): The zone round the centroid inside which the resultant keeps the whole base in contact: e ≤ L/6 on one axis; the rhombus 6e_x /L_x + 6e_y /L_y ≤ 1 for two.

[glossary-kicker] Glossary: kicker
kicker: A short length of column, about 75 mm, cast with the base to hold the column formwork; the starter-bar lap is measured from its top.

[glossary-pad-footing] Glossary: pad footing
pad footing: An isolated base, square or rectangular, under one column.

[glossary-partial-contact-lift-off] Glossary: partial contact (lift-off)
partial contact (lift-off): When e > L/6, part of the base leaves the soil; the pressure is a triangle over L_c . Special precautions once e > L/3 (EC7 6.5.4).

[glossary-pile-foundation] Glossary: pile foundation
pile foundation: Piles carry the load down to firm ground by end bearing, friction or both, through a pile cap (Units 11–12).

[glossary-punching-shear] Glossary: punching shear
punching shear: Failure of a slab or base round a concentrated load, on a truncated cone; checked on control perimeters (EC2 6.4).

[glossary-raft-foundation] Glossary: raft foundation
raft foundation: One slab under the whole building, for heavy loads, weak ground or variable soil.

[glossary-reduced-punching-force-v-ed-red] Glossary: reduced punching force V_{Ed,red}
reduced punching force V_{Ed,red}: N_{Ed} − p_{Ed} A: the column load less the soil pressure inside the perimeter (EC2 Eq. 6.48).

[glossary-self-weight-w] Glossary: self-weight W
self-weight W: The weight of the base, 25 kN/m³ × volume: in the bearing check, not in the bending and shear pressure.

[glossary-service-and-ultimate-loads] Glossary: service and ultimate loads
service and ultimate loads: G_k + Q_k for the soil (against q_{all} ); 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k for the concrete.

[glossary-settlement] Glossary: settlement
settlement: The downward movement of a foundation as the soil below it compresses.

[glossary-starter-bars] Glossary: starter bars
starter bars: Bars cast into the base with a 90° bend tied to the bottom mat, lapped with the column bars above the kicker.

[glossary-strap-footing] Glossary: strap footing
strap footing: A boundary pad tied by a strap beam to an inner footing so that the pair resists the overturning of the eccentric pad (Unit 11).

[glossary-strip-footing] Glossary: strip footing
strip footing: A continuous base under a wall or a row of columns, designed per metre run.

[glossary-v-min] Glossary: v_{min}
v_{min}: 0.035k^{3/2} f_{ck}^{1/2} : the shear resistance of concrete when no bars count; often the whole resistance of a footing.

[glossary-v-rd-max] Glossary: v_{Rd,max}
v_{Rd,max}: 0.4νf_{cd} , ν = 0.6(1 − f_{ck} /250): the strut limit at the column face (EC2 6.4.5(3), 2014 amendment; the course notes use 0.5νf_{cd} ).

[glossary-punching] Glossary: β (punching)
β (punching): 1 + k(M_{Ed} /V_{Ed} )(u/W): raises the punching stress for an unbalanced moment (EC2 6.4.3(3)).
